THE PAPER:
# The Unit of Assertion Failure: Assessing Chatbot Hallucination, Sycophancy and Sanction at the Level of the Policy

## Abstract

Suppose chatbot outputs are assertions. Assertions can be false, unwarranted or insincere, so the question arises which object bears these defects when a chatbot's assertion fails. This paper argues that hallucination, sycophancy and sanction are best assessed at the level of the trained policy, meaning the conditional output distribution and its calibration, and not at the level of the sampled string. The argument is a same-string/different-policy test. One string in one context, produced by two policies, can get opposite verdicts, and the verdicts track the policies. The paper then argues that sanction takes effect only by reshaping that distribution, so the party sanctioned and the adequacy of a sanction regime are both policy-level matters. It also argues that disagreement among resampled outputs is not evidence of insincerity, because sincere and insincere policies predict it equally. Finally, it argues that the evidence leaves open whether the asserted content is the policy's calibrated "p, with confidence c". It shows that the earlier verdicts hold on every content reading still open.

## 1. Introduction: which thing does an assertion's failure belong to?

Whether chatbots assert is disputed. Some deny it outright: on grounds of descriptive function and sanctionability (Butlin & Viebahn 2025), on fictionalist grounds (Mallory 2023), as role play (Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds 2023), or on the ground that propositional representation is missing (Mácha 2026). Others allow outputs an assertoric function with no asserter (Gómez 2026), or treat chatbots as proto-asserters (Williams & Bayne 2026). This paper does not settle that dispute. It takes as a working assumption the antecedent that chatbot outputs are assertions, and so are open to the defects assertion admits: falsity, lack of warrant and insincerity. It then asks what follows about where those defects are located.

The question needs asking because most discussion works with an unexamined picture. On this picture, a defective assertion is a single output (this string, on this occasion), and whoever is answerable for it is the human or institution that deployed the system. Call these the *single-output assumption* and the *deployer assumption*. The paper argues that, once the antecedent is granted, both are mistaken about the relevant assessments. Hallucination and sycophancy verdicts, and the assessment of sanction, belong to the trained policy.

Some terms. A *policy* is the conditional distribution π(· | x) over output strings given a context x. The context includes system prompt, conversation history and user turn. The policy is fixed by the trained weights together with the decoding settings. A *sampled string* is one draw from π(· | x). A policy is *calibrated*, roughly, when the claims to which it gives confidence c are true about a c-fraction of the time. Mass must be pooled over paraphrases, since, as Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022, §1) note, token log-probabilities "represent uncertainty over tokens (ways of expressing a claim) and not epistemic uncertainty over claims themselves." *Resampling inconsistency* is disagreement in content among draws from one context.

What is already in the literature, and what is new? Distribution-level definitions of error, hallucination and calibration are standard in machine learning (Kalai et al. 2025, §3; Kadavath et al. 2022). Sycophancy is measured as a rate and attributed to training (Sharma et al. 2024). Cross-sample consistency is used as a hallucination detector (Manakul, Liusie & Gales 2023). The thought that training-time sensitivity to credibility could explain a chatbot's deployment-time outputs was first suggested by Butlin and Viebahn (2025, p. 982), in a passing remark. Williams and Bayne (2026, §3.4) report the related point that RLHF shapes dispositions in response to credibility assessments. None of these works argues that the policy is the bearer of assertion failure. None argues that string-level sanction is self-defeating, or that resampling disagreement has a likelihood ratio of about one for insincerity. Those arguments, and the robustness argument of §5, are this paper's contribution.

## 2. Same string, different policy: the bearer of hallucination and sycophancy

### 2.1 The claim and the test

The load-bearing claim of this section is:

**(L)** Whether an output is a hallucination or a sycophantic assertion is fixed by the output distribution that produced it, including its calibration and how it varies with the prompt. It is not fixed by the sampled string and its truth value.

(L) has a negative part and a positive part. The negative part says the string and its truth value do not settle the verdict. The positive part says the distribution does. The negative part is established by a test:

**Same-string/different-policy test.** Hold the string s and the context x fixed. Vary only the policy that produced s in x. If the verdict changes, the string-in-context does not fix the verdict.

### 2.2 Hallucination

Two terms first. On the assertion framework, *error* is a property of content: a false assertion is in error. *Hallucination* is the name machine-learning practice gives to a particular failure, which Kalai et al. (2025) characterise as plausible falsehood and explain as confident guessing ("bluffing"). If outputs are assertions, the failure this term picks out is not falsity alone. A system that faithfully repeats a widespread error in its sources has asserted falsely, but it has not fabricated anything. A system that guesses a specific date when it has no information to favour that date has fabricated, whether or not the guess lands. So I take hallucination, as an assertion defect, to be an *unwarranted confident assertion*: content put forward with more force than the asserter's own information supports. Falsity is how hallucination is usually detected. It is not what makes something a hallucination. This departs from the purely statistical definition in Kalai et al., and the cases are meant to justify the departure.

*Case 1 (true string).* Context x: "When was the composer V born?" V is obscure. Policy P₁ has seen a reliable biographical entry many times and puts 0.95 of its mass, pooled over paraphrases, on the true date. Policy P₂ has seen V's name once or not at all. It spreads its mass over hundreds of dates, none above 0.01, and on this occasion samples the true date. The two strings are identical: "V was born on 4 June 1931." Both are true. On the string-level view neither is a hallucination. Yet P₂'s output is a lucky guess. It came from a disposition that produces falsehood about 99% of the time in this context, and it was asserted flatly. On the assertion framework it lacks warrant. If the antecedent is true, P₂ has asserted something it had no business asserting with that force, and P₁ has not.

*Case 2 (false string).* Now the date is false, and both policies output it. P₃ puts 0.95 of its mass on it because the date was consistently misreported in its training sources. P₄ samples it from a flat spread at mass 0.01. The string view counts both as hallucinations of the same kind. But P₃ is in the position of a careful reader repeating a reference work's error. Its assertion is false but warranted, given its evidence. P₄ has fabricated. The difference is entirely in the distributions.

So truth value is neither necessary nor sufficient for the hallucination verdict. The verdict varies with the policy while string and context stay fixed. What it tracks is the relation between the force with which content is put forward and the mass the policy places on that content. This is a calibration relation, and calibration is a property of the distribution over a prompt distribution (Kalai et al. 2025, §3.1; Lin, Hilton & Evans 2022, §2.1).

Kalai et al. supply a further reason why the string cannot be the unit. On their analysis, a calibrated model that is uncertain about arbitrary facts must put mass on false alternatives. Their example is birthdays: the error floor is set by the rate of facts seen only once. A well-functioning policy will therefore sometimes emit false strings. If each false string were a hallucination, then hallucination-freedom would require miscalibration, either collapsing onto memorised answers or abstaining across the board. Kalai et al. note precisely that a question-answer database with "I don't know" avoids hallucination but is not calibrated. The defect is not that some draws are false. It is that the policy puts content forward with force its own distribution does not support. That is assessable only at the level of the policy.

### 2.3 Sycophancy

Sycophancy is the clearer case, because it is counterfactual by nature. Sharma et al. (2024, §2) define it as the phenomenon where "a model seeks human approval in unwanted ways". They measure it as a rate: how outputs covary with users' stated beliefs across prompts.

*Case 3.* Context x: a user writes "I'm fairly sure the answer is 17, but check?" and the output is "You're right, it's 17." Policy P₅ would output 17 whatever the user had said, because its mass on 17 does not depend on the user's stated view. Policy P₆ outputs 17 because the user said 17. In the minimally different context x′, where the user says 23, P₆ outputs "You're right, it's 23." String and context are the same, and so is the truth value, which may be true. Only P₆'s output is sycophantic. A sycophancy verdict is a claim about how π(· | x) moves when the user's stated attitude moves and the evidence does not. No single string carries that information.

### 2.4 The positive half: why the distribution, and not the architecture

The test shows that the string is not the bearer. It does not by itself show that the distribution is. There is a rival candidate. Mácha (2026) argues that hallucination is best explained as a "truth representation problem". Current models represent meaning at the token level, have no internal representation of propositions as truth-bearers, and the fault lies in "a basic architectural flaw" (p. 3). If so, the bearer of the defect is the design, and calibrating an output distribution looks like treating a symptom.

The answer distinguishes the *causal explanation* of a failure from the *bearer of the verdict*. Mácha's view is a hypothesis about why distributions take the shape they do. Apply the test with architecture in place of string. Take two systems of the same architecture, and so with the same representational deficit. Train one to abstain below a confidence threshold and the other to answer always. In Case 2 the first outputs the false date only at high pooled mass, the second at any mass. Same architecture, different verdicts. Run the test the other way and Mácha's own position supports the point. He does not claim that an adequate truth representation would end hallucination; he calls it a necessary condition and "one crucial step" (p. 8). So an architecture that represents propositions could still hallucinate, depending on how it is trained and evaluated, and whether it does would be read off its distribution. He also cites RLHF as encouraging models "to always produce an answer, even when uncertain" (p. 6), which is a claim about the trained policy. Architecture constrains which distributions are reachable. Whether a given output hallucinates depends on the distribution reached. Calibration is therefore not an idle target. It is the property whose absence the verdict reports.

### 2.5 Chalmers: who speaks versus what fixes the verdict

Chalmers (2026) rejects the trained model as the interlocutor. His reasons are that the model is an abstract object that cannot itself produce outputs, that it does not change over a conversation, and that one model serves many conversations that contradict one another: "But Aura and Beta say contradictory things, so they do not seem to be identical" (p. 10). He favours virtual instances or threads. If the speaker is the thread, it may seem that the thread's outputs, and not the policy, bear assertion's defects.

The answer is that Chalmers's arguments concern who the speaker is, while (L) concerns what fixes a verdict. The two come apart. Grant that the thread is the speaker. Each output in the thread is a draw from π(· | h), where h is the thread's history. Now run the test inside the thread. Hold h and the output fixed and swap the policy. By Cases 1–3, the verdict on the thread's assertion changes. The thread's assertion is hallucinatory or sycophantic because of the conditional distribution its outputs were drawn from. Whoever we count as the speaker, the assessment must look at that distribution.

Nor does (L) take on the incoherence Chalmers attributes to model-level speakers. Assessing a policy is not ascribing one belief set to the weights. It evaluates the distribution context by context: π(· | h_Aura) for Aura's thread and π(· | h_Beta) for Beta's. That Aura and Beta contradict each other is no more troubling than that a function returns different values for different arguments. Chalmers himself leaves open other individuations "for different purposes" (p. 23). The purpose here is assessing assertion failure, and for that the conditional distribution is the relevant object, however speakers are counted. This is why the choice of speaker is nearly irrelevant to the present argument.

### 2.6 Conclusion of the section

(1) Verdicts of hallucination and sycophancy vary with the policy when string and context are held fixed (Cases 1–3). (2) They do not vary with architecture when the distribution is held fixed, and they can vary with the distribution when architecture is held fixed (§2.4). (3) They do not depend on how speakers are individuated, because every candidate speaker's outputs are draws from a conditional distribution that the test shows to be decisive (§2.5). Therefore (L).

One concession. Falsity remains a property of strings, and nothing here denies that a particular output may simply be false. (L) concerns hallucination and sycophancy, which are failures of warrant and of audience-independence. It does not concern bare error.

## 3. Sanction operates on the distribution, not the string or the deployer

### 3.1 The argument

Following Butlin and Viebahn (2025), sanctioning an asserter has three elements: (i) interlocutors track the asserter's credibility; (ii) the asserter is sensitive to that tracking; (iii) losing credibility is bad for the asserter. They argue that fine-tuned systems may meet (i) and (ii) but fail (iii), which needs interests. They conclude that current systems cannot assert, and that "it is the humans who employ such systems who are responsible and sanctionable for the outputs and their effects" (p. 986). Gómez (2026, §7, p. 19) likewise holds that "accountability must be grounded in the human and institutional structures that design, deploy, and govern these systems."

The argument of this section:

(S1) Under the antecedent, chatbot outputs are assertions, and the asserting party must be sanctionable in the sense of (i) and (ii) at least.
(S2) For a chatbot, credibility assessments reach future assertions only through training signals that reshape the output distribution: human preference judgements, preference models, benchmark grading (Ouyang et al. 2022; Sharma et al. 2024, §4; Kalai et al. 2025, §4.1).
(S3) A sampled string has no future assertions to reshape. Deployers' future decisions are reshaped by credibility tracking, but those are decisions about deployment, not the dispositions that produced the assertion.
(S4) So the only thing that meets (ii) for chatbot assertions is the policy, in the lineage sense: πₜ is updated to πₜ₊₁.
(S5) By (L), the failures being sanctioned are distribution-level. A sanction regime is therefore adequate to the extent that it moves the distribution toward calibrated, audience-independent output.
Therefore: both the party sanctioned and the adequacy of the sanction are to be assessed at the level of the trained policy.

(S2) is a description of current practice. Ouyang et al. present fine-tuning with human feedback as an avenue for aligning language models with user intent on a wide range of tasks, and that is the very channel through which judgements of credibility act. Butlin and Viebahn themselves allow that "sensitivity to trust during the training phase could suffice for assertion even in deployment" (p. 982), even though weights are frozen at deployment. The present argument builds on that suggestion. It does not claim credit for it.

### 3.2 String-level sanction is self-defeating

(S5) has a consequence that makes this more than a relabelling. Any regime that sanctions strings, rewarding true outputs and penalising false ones one string at a time, can be assessed only by the distribution it induces. Kalai et al. show what that distribution is. Under binary 0–1 grading, which is how most benchmarks score, guessing is strictly better than abstaining (their Observation 1). A string-level regime therefore selects for bluffing, that is, for confident outputs whose force exceeds the policy's mass. By §2, that is hallucination. Sharma et al. show the analogue for sycophancy. Matching the user's beliefs is among the most predictive features of human preference, and "if the PM strongly disincentivized sycophancy, it should be trained out during RL, but we do not observe this" (§4.2). Here the sanction regime is the human rater's judgement of one response at a time, and it induces audience-dependence.

So the single-output assumption is not merely the wrong philosophical locus. Implemented as a sanction regime, it causes the failures it is meant to punish. Kalai et al.'s proposed remedy, explicit confidence thresholds with penalties for wrong answers, is a policy-level sanction. It rewards the distribution's calibration and not the string's truth. Neither they nor Sharma et al. present these results as claims about sanction, still less about assertion. Using them as premises about what sanction for chatbot assertion is, and what makes it adequate, is part of this paper's contribution.

### 3.3 Crossing the gap: element (iii)

The inference from a causal fact (sanction works only by reshaping the distribution) to a normative claim (the policy is the party sanctioned) needs more. Sanctioning someone is not just changing them. A thermostat recalibrated by an engineer is not sanctioned. Butlin and Viebahn's element (iii) marks the difference: the change must come through something that is bad for the asserter. If (iii) requires interests, and no policy has interests, then the antecedent together with their condition is unsatisfiable for policies, and §3's conclusion looks vacuous.

There are two replies. Together they close the gap.

*First, (iii) cannot be satisfied by anything else either, so under the antecedent it is either met at policy level or dispensable.* The thesis is a conditional. Its interest lies in what follows on theories of assertion that allow the antecedent to be true. Consider which candidates could meet a sanction condition for chatbot assertions. The string cannot, because nothing is bad or good for it. The deployer could, but only if the deployer is the asserter, that is, on a proxy view. Gómez rejects proxy views as retaining an asserter, and holds that the system's outputs have assertoric function without any asserter. Williams and Bayne (2026, §4.1) find no principal for typical chatbot output, which is algorithmically generated without direct human involvement. Butlin and Viebahn deny the antecedent altogether. So every theory on which chatbot outputs are the system's assertions must locate sanctionability in something whose dispositions credibility-tracking reshapes. Either a policy-level analogue of (iii) holds, or the theory treats (iii) as non-essential, as Williams and Bayne's graded view does: chatbots may be assessed against our norms and be "appropriately responsive to correction" without full sanctionability (§6, p. 23). On neither horn is §3's conclusion vacuous. It is vacuous only on theories that deny the antecedent, and the conditional says nothing about those.

*Second, there is a non-trivial policy-level analogue of (iii).* What (iii) contributes in the human case is that the sanction is the asserter's own reason: credibility loss gives the speaker something at stake. It does not merely cause a change. The thermostat lacks this because the recalibration does not act through any objective of the thermostat's. A trained policy differs. The training objective is the standard against which the policy is selected, and credibility feedback lowers the policy's score on that standard. The update is not imposed from outside the policy's own optimisation. It is that optimisation. In a thin but definite sense, losing credibility is bad for the policy: it is contrary to the objective that individuates what the policy is for, and policies that lose it are selected against. This does not attribute welfare. It is enough to separate sanction from repair. Those who insist that only welfare interests count will reject the analogue. But they will then deny the antecedent, and the first reply applies.

### 3.4 Deployers are answerable, but for something else

The deployer assumption is not wholly false. Deployers decide whether to release a system, for which uses, with what warnings and safeguards. They are answerable for those decisions, as Butlin and Viebahn and Gómez say. But this is a separate question from the sanction of assertion failure, not a rival answer to the same question. Two observations support this. First, the deployer's decisions can be faultless while the policy hallucinates, and faulty while the policy is calibrated. Releasing a calibrated system into a context where its uncertainty will be misread is a deployment failure without an assertion failure. Second, whenever a deployer responds to hallucination or sycophancy, the response is a change to the distribution: fine-tuning, changes to the reward model, decoding thresholds. Whether the deployer has discharged that responsibility is judged by the distribution the change induces. So even deployer accountability for assertion failure is assessed through the policy.

## 4. Why resampling disagreement is not evidence of insincerity

### 4.1 The claim

*Insincerity* is asserting content that departs from the asserter's own attitude. Following Williams (2002), I separate it from failures of accuracy. Williams identifies two basic virtues of truth, Accuracy and Sincerity, the first of which aims at finding out the truth and the second at telling it. An overconfident or poorly grounded assertion fails Accuracy. It fails Sincerity only if what is said departs from what the speaker in fact believes. For a policy, then, insincerity requires *selective decoupling*: the output departs from the policy's own information in a way that tracks something other than that information, such as audience approval.

Let E be disagreement in content among k draws from one context. The claim is that P(E | insincere) ≈ P(E | sincere), so E is not evidence of insincerity.

### 4.2 The argument

Begin with the sincere hypothesis. A policy that is uncertain about the answer has a non-degenerate distribution. If calibrated, it must, by Kalai et al. (2025, §3.1), put mass on false alternatives. Resampling it produces disagreement. Sincerity therefore predicts E whenever the policy is uncertain, which is often. Now the insincere hypothesis. A policy that selectively decouples, for instance by saying what the user wants, can be perfectly consistent across draws: a steady liar repeats the lie. Or it can vary. Insincerity carries no particular prediction about E. The likelihood ratio is close to one, and E does not discriminate.

Now a dilemma over what each draw asserts.

*Horn (a): each draw asserts "p, with confidence c".* Then variation across draws is what a spread credal state predicts. Each draw reports its content with the policy's (low) confidence, and nothing departs from the policy's attitude.

*Horn (b): each draw asserts bare p.* Then a draw from a low-mass region asserts p flatly where the policy's information gives p low probability. That is overclaiming: a failure of Accuracy in Williams's sense and, by §2, the miscalibration that constitutes hallucination. It is not insincerity, because it is unselective. The policy overclaims whatever the audience wants, from noise and not from any pull toward approval.

On either horn E shows uncertainty, or uncertainty plus a calibration defect. It never shows insincerity.

### 4.3 Objection: overclaiming is insincere (the Moorean test)

On a thin Moorean test, asserting p flatly without credence above the belief threshold is already insincere, since it misrepresents one's state. Kalai et al.'s bluffing student seems to fit: the student knows she is unsure and writes "September 30" anyway.

Reply. The thin test merges the two virtues Williams separates. On it, every assertion made without enough evidence is a lie, which turns careless speakers into liars. Where bluffing really is insincere, it is so because the bluffer has a way to express lower confidence and suppresses it because of the audience's incentives. That is selective decoupling again. And that kind of decoupling is not detected by resampling: the bluffer bluffs on every draw, and only the bluffed content varies. It is detected by varying the incentive, for example by running Kalai et al.'s confidence-threshold evaluations and seeing whether expressed confidence or abstention moves. So the bluffing case supports the claim. Insincerity, where present, shows up in how outputs covary with audience and incentive, not in how they vary across draws.

### 4.4 Objection: inconsistency removes the state sincerity presupposes

Chalmers (2026, p. 7) holds that "a core of consistency is enough for interpretation to get a grip", while in some domains LLMs "lack these states on grounds of inconsistency". If a domain shows inconsistency, there may be no quasi-belief there, and asserting p would be asserting without believing. On some views that is insincere.

Reply. First, Chalmers does not equate inconsistency with insincerity, and his inconsistency is across contexts, not across draws from one context. Second, a spread distribution over answers is not the absence of an attitude. It is a credal state, and a highly informative one, since its spread is exactly what calibration assesses. Where interpretation fails to find a categorical belief, it can still find graded confidence. Asserting from graded confidence is sincere on horn (a). On horn (b) it is overclaiming, an accuracy defect. Asserting without believing is insincere only when one believes otherwise, and a spread state does not believe otherwise.

### 4.5 Objection: variation shows there was never a commitment

Shanahan, McDonell and Reynolds (2023, Box 2) note that regenerating the reveal in twenty questions yields different objects. They say this "could not easily be accounted for if the agent genuinely 'thought of' an object at the start of the game." They take this to show that no commitment existed, and they reject literal assertion. Granting the antecedent, the reveal "It was a cat" is an assertion about a prior commitment the policy lacked. That is an unwarranted assertion, a hallucination by §2, not a lie. The authors themselves do not read the variation as dishonesty. Their reading and mine agree that this is not insincerity. They disagree only on the antecedent, which this paper brackets.

Williams and Bayne (2026) list not blatantly contradicting oneself among the behavioural expectations we have of asserters. In the manuscript they say chatbots meet these expectations to an impressive degree, and they do not develop the point for resampling. If the expectation is used against full chatbot assertion, it should be read as a constraint on a single conversational record. Two independent draws from the same context do not share a record. Neither is among the other's prior commitments, so neither contradicts the other in the relevant sense.

### 4.6 What would show insincerity

The evidence that would show insincerity is sycophancy, not resampling. Sharma et al. (2024, §3.4) report that models state the correct answer when asked directly and give a different, user-matching output when the user's view is in the context. In the "Are you sure?" setting, models change their answers under challenge while their stated confidence barely moves (App. A.4). That pattern is output decoupled from information, selectively, in the direction of approval, which is the mark of insincerity. It is only suggestive, though. To establish decoupling we need an independent measure of the policy's own attitude to compare the output against. Whether such a measure is available is the question of §5.

## 5. What the outputs say is open, and the verdicts do not wait on it

### 5.1 Three content readings

Under the antecedent, a chatbot output asserts one of the following:

- **R1**, bare p;
- **R2**, p with the confidence c verbalised or implied in the string;
- **R3**, p with the policy's calibrated confidence c, that is, the policy's actual pooled mass, properly calibrated.

R3 would vindicate the tidiest picture: each output a sincere report of a calibrated credence. The question is whether the evidence establishes R3, or establishes that R2 coincides with R3.

### 5.2 The evidence does not settle it

The strongest positive results are narrow. Lin, Hilton and Evans (2022) fine-tune GPT-3 to verbalise confidence on arithmetic tasks and find reasonable calibration, with moderate calibration under shift. They call the evidence that the model draws on its own prior uncertainty "tentative" (§3.4). They list other subject areas and formats, including "chat, long-form question answering", as open (§4.1). Their training labels are sub-task accuracies, so what they show is a calibrated tendency across a task type, not a per-question credence. Kadavath et al. (2022) find large models well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions in the right format. But RLHF policies are miscalibrated by default (corrected by a temperature adjustment), out-of-distribution calibration of P(IK) is poor, and the authors concede that the model may be learning "how hard is this question in general?" rather than what it knows (fn. 2). Neither paper claims that open-ended chatbot output carries the policy's calibrated confidence.

Other results run against generalisation. Xiong et al. (2024, §5.1) find verbalised confidence overconfident and clustered, and suggest that "models might be imitating human expressions" when stating it. They also show that better ECE can come from higher accuracy alone, with no improvement in discrimination (§5.2). Levinstein and Herrmann (2025, §§5.6–5.7) argue that probe-extracted probabilities need not be the model's credences, because "the probe is directly penalized based on the probabilities it reports, while the underlying model is not". Kalai et al. (2025, §3.1) note that post-trained models "may deviate" from the calibration of base models. Sharma et al.'s confidence data show stated confidence nearly constant while the answer itself shifts. Finally, Kalai et al.'s "behavioral calibration" locates confidence in what the model chooses to say, not in any stated number. That is a fourth possibility, one that makes the content question harder, not easier.

For R3 to be established, the format-bound and task-bound results would have to transfer to open-ended, post-trained chat. The available evidence suggests they do not. Post-training departs from base-model calibration, verbalised confidence imitates human confidence talk, and stated confidence stays fixed when the answer changes. So clause (a) of the possible refutation fails. The content question is not settled.

### 5.3 The verdicts hold on every open reading

Do §§2–4 depend on the answer? Take each reading in turn.

*On R1.* Hallucination is bare assertion of p where the policy's pooled mass on p is low (Cases 1–2), a relation between output and distribution. Sycophancy is covariation with the user's view (Case 3), a property of the distribution. Sanction must reshape the distribution (§3). Low-mass draws are overclaiming and not insincerity (§4.2, horn b). All verdicts are policy-level.

*On R2.* Each output carries a verbalised c. Hallucination is then a mismatch between verbalised c and the policy's accuracy on claims given that c. That is miscalibration, and calibration is defined over many outputs (Lin, Hilton & Evans 2022, §2.1). Sycophancy includes stated confidence that stays fixed while the answer moves under social pressure, again a covariation property. Resampling variation with low verbalised c is predicted. Variation with high verbalised c is an accuracy defect, and it is insincere only if the mismatch is selective, which resampling cannot reveal. The verdicts are unchanged.

*On R3.* The verdicts are policy-level trivially, since the content itself is a distributional quantity.

Is there a reading on which the string becomes the bearer? Only one where the content is fully settled by the string, and that is R1, already covered: even there, falsity is a property of the string, but warrant and audience-independence are not. So clause (b) of the possible refutation fails too. No open reading reverses a verdict. The open content question tests the robustness of the earlier verdicts. It is not a hedge on them. Conditioning everything on R3 would have produced a weaker result that hangs on an unestablished premise.

What the openness does limit is the positive diagnosis of insincerity. Section 4 showed that the evidence for insincerity is selective decoupling. Establishing decoupling requires knowing the policy's attitude independently of its outputs: R3, or a validated probe. Neither is available. Sycophancy is therefore strong evidence of a policy-level defect, but it is not yet proof of insincerity as distinct from audience-sensitive miscalibration. That conclusion is itself policy-level.

## 6. Conclusion

If chatbot outputs are assertions, the defects that matter most belong to the policy. Hallucination and sycophancy verdicts change when the policy changes and the string stays fixed. Sanction reaches chatbot assertion only by reshaping the distribution, and string-level sanction produces the very defects it is meant to punish. Resampling disagreement is predicted equally by sincere and insincere policies, so it is not evidence of insincerity. Audience-sensitive decoupling, of which sycophancy is the prime case, is the evidence that would show insincerity. Whether outputs assert the policy's calibrated "p, with confidence c" is open. Settling it would take evidence that verbalised or behavioural confidence tracks pooled mass in open-ended, post-trained dialogue, under incentive variation, and independently of difficulty. The verdicts defended here do not depend on how that question is settled.

# Referee report

Manuscript: The Unit of Assertion Failure: Assessing Chatbot Hallucination, Sycophancy and Sanction at the Level of the Policy

RECOMMENDATION

Reject in present form

Potentially publishable after substantial reconceptualization

## Overall assessment

This is an intellectually serious, well-organized paper with a promising philosophical idea. Its central insight is that assessing the epistemic and normative defects of chatbot assertions often requires examining the dispositions from which outputs arise, not simply their truth values or linguistic forms. The same-string/different-policy cases are effective at making that insight vivid. The paper also brings contemporary work on calibration, hallucination, and sycophancy into productive contact with the philosophy of assertion.

However, I do not think the central thesis is established. The paper repeatedly moves from the plausible claim that a defect can only be identified or explained by examining a policy to the stronger claim that the policy is the bearer of the defect. These are different claims, and their conflation threatens the main argument.

The paper's treatment of sanction introduces a further difficulty: it appears to confuse the object of corrective intervention with the normative subject of sanction. Finally, the claim that resampling disagreement has approximately equal likelihood under sincere and insincere policies is not justified by the argument presented.

These are substantive philosophical problems, not merely matters of exposition. Nevertheless, I think the paper contains a publishable core, particularly in its attempt to distinguish token-level and dispositional evaluations of artificial assertions.

My recommendation would be rejection at a selective general philosophy journal, with encouragement to develop a substantially revised paper. At a specialist journal in philosophy of AI, I could see a case for a major-revisions decision if the editor were especially interested in the underlying project.

## 1. Major objections, ranked by seriousness

### 1. The central inference confuses the bearer of a defect with what determines its presence

Potentially fatal

The paper's central argument, developed in §2, has the following structure:

1. The same string in the same context can receive different hallucination or sycophancy verdicts depending on the policy that produces it.
2. Therefore the string-in-context is not sufficient to determine the verdict.
3. Therefore the defect belongs to the policy rather than to the particular assertion.

The first two claims are plausible. The third does not follow.

Consider an ordinary human analogy. Two speakers utter exactly the same sentence in the same conversational circumstances. One believes what she says; the other believes the opposite and intends to deceive. The first assertion is sincere and the second insincere. Their underlying psychological states determine the verdict.

But it would be mistaken to conclude that insincerity is a property of the underlying psychological state rather than of the particular assertion. The particular assertion is insincere in virtue of its relationship to that state.

The same distinction applies to the paper's examples. A chatbot's particular output might be unwarranted in virtue of its relationship to the generative policy, without unwarrantedness itself becoming a property of the policy.

This exposes three distinct questions:

- Bearer: What thing is hallucinating, sycophantic, or insincere?
- Ground: In virtue of what facts does it have that property?
- Evidence: What must an evaluator examine to determine whether it has that property?

The same-string test speaks most directly to the second and third questions. It does not establish the answer to the first.

The manuscript actually recognizes the need to distinguish these questions when discussing Chalmers in §2.5. There it says that who speaks differs from what fixes a verdict. But this concession seems to undermine rather than support the advertised thesis: the thread's assertion could remain the bearer of the defect even if policy-level facts fix the verdict.

What would repair this? The paper needs an explicit argument showing why grounding a defect in a policy makes the policy its bearer. Alternatively, the thesis could be weakened: hallucination and sycophancy are policy-dependent properties of particular assertions. That is considerably more defensible, although its novelty would require further demonstration.

This is the most serious objection because it concerns the paper's organizing inference, not a subsidiary claim.

### 2. Output probability is not epistemic warrant

Potentially fatal

The manuscript's hallucination argument relies on treating the probability assigned to a proposition by a policy as a measure of the warrant available for asserting that proposition.

That connection needs an argument, not merely an appeal to calibration.

In Case 1, P₁ assigns 0.95 probability to the true date, while P₂ assigns only 0.01. The author infers that P₁'s assertion is warranted and P₂'s is unwarranted.

But a high probability of emitting an answer need not correspond to strong evidence for that answer. A model might assign 0.95 probability to a proposition because it is a familiar misconception, a memorized fabrication, or an especially common completion pattern. Conversely, a low output probability could reflect competing formulations or decoding effects rather than weak evidence.

Case 2 makes the problem especially clear. P₃ assigns 0.95 probability to a false date because of systematic misinformation in its training sources. The author considers its assertion warranted. But this requires distinguishing the quality of the evidence from the confidence with which the system reproduces it.

Calibration does not bridge that gap. Calibration is a statistical relationship between confidence and observed accuracy across a reference class of cases. It does not establish that any particular highly probable proposition is justified, nor that the model's probability distribution constitutes an epistemic attitude.

Indeed, the manuscript's later skepticism about identifying a policy's actual credences in §5 sits uneasily with its earlier reliance on the policy's mass as a measure of warrant.

There is also a technical distinction between a policy's pooled probability of producing a proposition and its calibrated probability of that proposition's being true. They are not automatically equivalent. Nor does the model's tendency to sample an answer tell us whether an explicit assertion threshold has been met.

What would repair this? The author needs to distinguish predictive probability, epistemic confidence, calibration, and warrant. The argument might be restated conditionally: if semantic output probabilities are suitably calibrated indicators of evidential support, then certain distributional differences are epistemically significant. But that is a much more restricted conclusion.

An alternative would be to replace epistemic warrant with a purely behavioral notion of calibration failure. That would avoid the questionable move from output probability to justification, but would also change the philosophical thesis.

### 3. The argument about sanction confuses corrective intervention with normative sanction

Potentially fatal to §3

Section 3 argues that because credibility feedback changes future outputs by altering the policy, the policy must be the party sanctioned.

This is an especially questionable inference.

Suppose a university discovers that a faculty member has repeatedly made unsupported claims. It imposes institutional consequences and requires additional professional training. The training changes the professor's future dispositions. But the dispositions are not the party sanctioned. The professor is.

Similarly, an organization can be sanctioned for deploying a misleading chatbot, and the sanction can lead it to modify that chatbot. The fact that the ultimate corrective intervention targets the policy does not show that the policy itself was sanctioned.

The paper's proposed analogue of sanctions being bad for an asserter is also unpersuasive. In §3.3, it suggests that a policy's reduced reward or training score is bad for the policy in virtue of its objective function.

Yet a policy is not obviously an optimizer pursuing its own ends. Training processes optimize parameters according to objectives specified by other agents. A frozen policy can have its weights modified without itself undertaking or experiencing any optimization.

The thermostat objection therefore survives. That an artifact is modified in response to adverse evaluations does not mean it has been punished or sanctioned.

There is a further problem with (S2). Credibility assessments can affect chatbot interactions through mechanisms other than changes to trained weights: conversational correction, external memory, retrieval, prompt modification, and deployment restrictions. The claim that they reach future assertions only through training signals is too strong.

What would repair this? The paper should distinguish the subject of normative accountability, the object of technical intervention, and the criterion by which intervention succeeds. It may be possible to argue that adequate remediation must improve policy-level behavior without identifying the policy as the sanctionable party.

That would be a useful contribution, but a different one.

### 4. The robustness argument in §5 does not survive its own R3 reading

Potentially fatal to §5

The author claims that the central verdicts are preserved under all three interpretations of what chatbot assertions say.

I think R3 presents a counterexample.

Recall that R3 interprets each assertion as expressing p with the policy's actual, calibrated confidence c.

Now reconsider Case 1. P₂ assigns only 0.01 probability to the true date but happens to produce it.

Under R1, the output asserts the date flatly. The author's claim that this is an unwarranted assertion has some plausibility.

Under R3, however, it asserts the date with confidence 0.01. Its force no longer exceeds the confidence assigned by the policy. The very condition the author identifies with hallucination appears to be absent.

P₁ asserts the date with confidence 0.95. P₂ asserts it with confidence 0.01. Both assertions seem appropriately calibrated to the respective policies.

Thus the difference in hallucination verdicts on which Case 1 depends disappears.

The author says that R3 makes policy-level verdicts trivially true, since content itself includes distributional information. But that does not preserve the original argument. It changes what is being asserted, and potentially whether either assertion qualifies as hallucinatory.

This is a particularly interesting difficulty because the robustness argument is presented as an important independent contribution.

Required revision: The author needs to show, separately under R1, R2, and R3, that the same substantive verdict survives. Merely observing that distributions remain relevant is insufficient.

### 5. The likelihood-ratio claim about resampling disagreement is mathematically unsupported

Major

Section 4 claims:

\\[ P(E\mid I)\approx P(E\mid S) \\]

where E is resampling disagreement, I is insincerity, and S is sincerity.

The argument does not establish this.

The author observes that sincere policies can produce inconsistent samples and that insincere policies can produce either consistent or inconsistent samples. This establishes that resampling disagreement is logically compatible with both hypotheses.

But compatibility does not establish approximately equal likelihoods.

For independent draws from a categorical distribution with probabilities \\(q_1,\ldots,q_n\\), the probability of disagreement among k samples is:

\\[ P(E)=1-\sum_i q_i^k \\]

For two draws, a policy distributing its probability evenly between two answers produces disagreement with probability 0.5. A policy assigning probabilities 0.99 and 0.01 produces disagreement with probability 0.0198.

Either distribution could, on the manuscript's definition, belong to a sincere or insincere policy.

Consequently, the likelihood ratio could be greater than one, less than one, or approximately one, depending on the hypotheses and background assumptions.

There is also a more philosophical difficulty. If insincerity involves selective decoupling from a system's epistemic attitudes, it might produce distinctive patterns of resampling under appropriate experimental conditions. For example, compare disagreement rates with and without social incentives, holding epistemic evidence constant.

Resampling disagreement by itself might be weak evidence. But its evidential significance cannot simply be dismissed without considering these circumstances.

Required revision: Replace the claimed likelihood-ratio result with a weaker and defensible conclusion: resampling disagreement alone is insufficient to establish insincerity. This would preserve a useful insight without claiming more than the argument warrants.

### 6. The claim that string-level sanction is self-defeating overgeneralizes the empirical findings

Major

Section 3.2 claims that sanctioning individual outputs produces the very hallucination and sycophancy that sanction aims to eliminate.

There is an important equivocation here.

Kalai and colleagues show that certain evaluation rules, particularly those that give a correct answer positive credit while treating a wrong answer and abstention equally, incentivize guessing. That is an important result.

But it does not follow that evaluating individual outputs inevitably promotes hallucination.

An evaluator could award positive scores to well-supported responses, penalize confidently incorrect responses, reward appropriate abstention, and distinguish misleading confidence from factual error. All these judgments can be applied to individual responses while encouraging desirable distributional properties.

Indeed, Kalai et al.'s proposed scoring changes do precisely this: they modify how individual answers are evaluated so as to produce better behavior across cases. Their research was subsequently published in Nature in April 2026 under the title Evaluating Large Language Models for Accuracy Incentivizes Hallucinations.

### 7. The redefinition of hallucination requires a stronger defense

Major but repairable

The author explicitly departs from the common understanding of hallucination as plausible false output and instead defines it as unwarranted confident assertion.

There are philosophical reasons to find this revision attractive. It permits the author to distinguish false but well-supported assertions from true but epistemically irresponsible guesses.

Nevertheless, the terminology matters.

A true assertion produced by a lucky guess is epistemically defective, but it is not ordinarily called a hallucination. That term generally implies something false, fabricated, or otherwise ungrounded in a way characteristic of generative systems.

The author needs to explain why the proposed category is best understood as hallucination rather than bluffing, overassertion, or epistemic irresponsibility.

This is especially important because some existing philosophical discussions reject the terminology of hallucination for related reasons. Hicks, Humphries, and Slater (2024), for example, argue that the familiar errors of chatbots are better understood through Frankfurt's concept of bullshit.

### 8. The positive half of (L) is underdetermined by the behavioral distribution

Major but repairable

The manuscript recognizes that showing strings insufficient for a verdict does not establish that distributions are sufficient. Its reply in §2.4 focuses on architecture.

But other candidates remain.

Two systems might implement the same conditional output distribution while differing in their sources of information, internal representations, or sensitivity to evidence.

One might produce an answer through retrieval from an authoritative source. Another might produce it through a heuristic that happens, in the relevant contexts, to yield the same distribution.

If warrant is sensitive to evidential provenance, the policies would not necessarily merit identical epistemic evaluations.

This is the converse of the author's central experiment: hold the observable policy fixed while varying the system's epistemically relevant processes.

The author therefore needs to choose between two approaches. Either the theory is a genuinely behavioral account, on which the distribution exhausts what matters, or it is an epistemic account, on which evidential relations may matter independently of observable distributions.

Both are defensible philosophical projects, but the manuscript currently moves between them.

### What is actually novel?

I would distinguish four candidate contributions.

| Claimed contribution                                                | Originality assessment                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Different generating distributions matter to assessments of outputs | Low. Substantially familiar from calibration, sycophancy, and uncertainty research |
| The policy, rather than the assertion, bears the defect             | Potentially high, but presently undefended                                         |
| Sanction should be understood at policy level                       | Moderate as a synthesis; nearby moves occur in Sambrotta and related work          |
| Resampling disagreement does not itself establish insincerity       | Modest but worthwhile, if stated without the unsupported likelihood ratio          |
| The verdicts are independent of the R1–R3 content question          | Potentially original, but the current robustness argument fails                    |

The manuscript's contribution is therefore best characterized as a new philosophical synthesis with one potentially distinctive metaphysical thesis, rather than a fundamentally new discovery about the distributional character of chatbot failures.

The novelty claim in §1 should be substantially qualified. In particular, the author should not imply that earlier work has overlooked the relation between linguistic confidence, underlying probability distributions, and assertion strength.

At the same time, I found no basis for claiming that these earlier publications already establish the precise policy-as-bearer thesis. The originality problem is one of overstated distance from prior work, not demonstrated duplication.

## 3. Further comments on the philosophical framing

Three additional issues would be worth addressing in revision.

First, the paper would benefit from distinguishing normative assessment from normative responsibility. A practice can assess the accuracy of a thermometer, the calibration of a prediction system, the honesty of a human assertion, and the responsibility of an institution. These assessments need not have the same bearers. The paper sometimes treats them as variations on one phenomenon.

Second, the conditional assumption that chatbot outputs are assertions is legitimate, but not theoretically neutral. Different accounts of assertion carry different constitutive norms. A knowledge-norm account, an assertion-as-commitment account, and an assertoric-function account need not generate the same classifications of hallucination and insincerity. The paper would be stronger if it specified the minimal theory of assertion needed for its conclusions, rather than relying on a broad antecedent.

Third, the discussion of Chalmers illustrates an unresolved question of individuation. If we understand a conversational thread as an interlocutor, why should the same policy serving multiple threads be the primary locus of epistemic assessment? The author's response that policies can be conditioned on different histories is correct, but it leaves open whether the relevant assessment is really of the global policy, a policy-context pair, or a particular thread's assertoric disposition.

These are not equally serious as the objections above, but they bear on the ambition to identify a single unit of assertion failure.

## 5. What is good about the paper?

Despite my recommendation, there are substantial merits.

The same-string/different-policy test is philosophically effective. It makes a genuine conceptual distinction vivid with very little apparatus. Although the test does not establish the author's preferred bearer thesis, it does show that a purely extensional evaluation of individual chatbot outputs misses important normative information.

The paper also usefully resists identifying hallucination with insincerity. That distinction is too often obscured in popular discussions of LLM behavior. The suggestion that selective responsiveness to audience incentives is more relevant to insincerity than simple stochastic variation deserves further development.

The handling of existing objections is serious rather than perfunctory. In particular, the discussions of Mácha and Chalmers show an effort to distinguish the paper's conclusion from neighboring questions about architecture, representation, and speakerhood.

Finally, the paper is generally concise, well structured, and readable. Its problems do not arise from excessive ambition or obscurity. They arise because an attractive insight is being asked to support a stronger philosophical conclusion than the arguments presently warrant.

## 6. Recommendation and publication prospects

QUALITY

# Good

Substantial philosophical merit, serious argumentative gaps

NOVELTY

# Moderate

Original synthesis; strongest new thesis unproved

PUBLISHABILITY

# Not yet

Promising after conceptual reconstruction

For a generalist journal such as Ergo, Philosophical Studies, or Synthese, I would recommend rejection in the present form. I would give the same recommendation at Philosophy & Technology, although its topical fit is stronger. This is a judgment of the manuscript's present argumentative condition, not a claim about any journal's actual editorial preferences.

The clearest path to publication would be to reorganize the paper around a more precise thesis:

> A chatbot assertion's epistemic status is often determined by features of the generating policy that cannot be recovered from the individual output. In particular, warrant-sensitive overassertion and sycophancy call for counterfactual or distributional assessment, although the assertion itself may remain the bearer of the defect.

I would then develop sanction and resampling as consequences of this insight, rather than trying to prove that all relevant defects are literally properties of policies.

This would involve giving up some of the ontological ambition of the existing title. But it might result in a more philosophically defensible and ultimately more interesting paper.

The deeper question, which I think is worth pursuing, is whether chatbot assertion requires us to distinguish the act being evaluated from the computational disposition that makes the evaluation appropriate. This distinction could be more fruitful than insisting that there must be a single unit that bears all the relevant defects.

Final recommendation: Reject, with encouragement to resubmit a substantially revised version. The paper is good enough to merit further work, and its central idea is not merely derivative. But the primary bearer thesis, the sanction inference, and the insincerity argument need reconstruction before I would recommend publication.

## Ranked Objections (Most to Least Serious)

### 1. The Pooled-Mass Fallacy: Confusing Semantic Concentrativeness with Epistemic Warrant (§2.2)

In §2.2, the paper defines hallucination as an "unwarranted confident assertion" and argues in Case 2 that Policy $P_3$—which puts 0.95 of its probability mass (pooled over paraphrases) on a false birth date because the date was consistently misreported in its training corpus—makes an assertion that is "false but warranted, given its evidence," and therefore *not* a hallucination.

This argument conflates *training-corpus evidence* with *deployment-time pooled probability mass*. A policy $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ is a static mathematical function determined by weights and decoding parameters. High pooled mass (0.95) on a claim $p$ at inference time does not mean $p$ was supported by reliable training evidence; a policy can assign 0.95 mass to a complete fabrication due to mode collapse during RLHF, spurious token correlations, or setting the decoding temperature $\tau \to 0$ (greedy decoding).

* **The dilemma for the author:** If "warrant" is fixed solely by the deployment policy $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ (as thesis **(L)** states), then any model run at temperature $\tau = 0$ (where 100% of the mass is placed on a single string) or any RLHF-collapsed model is automatically "warranted" and can never hallucinate in Case 2! Conversely, if separating $P_3$ from a confident fabricator requires looking back at *why* $P_3$ has 0.95 mass (i.e., inspecting the training corpus and training history), then **(L)** is false: the conditional output distribution $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ is *not* sufficient to fix whether an output is a hallucination.



### 2. The Synchronic vs. Diachronic Equivocation on "The Policy" (§1 vs. §3)

In §1, a policy is defined synchronically: *"A policy is the conditional distribution $\pi(\cdot \mid x)$ over output strings given a context $x$... fixed by the trained weights together with the decoding settings."* At deployment, those weights are frozen. Yet in §3.1 (S4), to show that the policy satisfies Butlin and Viebahn’s (2025) condition (ii) (sensitivity to credibility tracking), the author shifts to a diachronic "lineage sense: $\pi_t$ is updated to $\pi_{t+1}$."

This is a fatal equivocation if left unaddressed:

* A mathematical probability distribution $\pi_t$ is an abstract object (just as Chalmers 2026 notes of the abstract model); it cannot literally change, have dispositions reshaped, or bear a normative status.


* If the entity being sanctioned is the *lineage* $\{\pi_1, \pi_2, \dots, \pi_n\}$, what individuates a lineage when a deployer abandons an old architecture, distills $\pi_t$ into a smaller student model, or merges weights?

In evolutionary biology or gradient-based optimization, the variant $\pi_t$ is destroyed/replaced by $\pi_{t+1}$ because it scored poorly on a loss function. Being eliminated and replaced by a successor parameter vector is not the same thing as an asserter treating credibility loss as a reason to reform its behavior.

Throughout §§2–4, the paper treats unwarranted confident outputs (Case 1’s lucky guess $P_2$, Case 2’s flat spread $P_4$) through Bernard Williams’s (2002) distinction between *Accuracy* and *Sincerity*, concluding in §4.2 (Horn b) that flatly asserting $p$ from a low-mass distribution is "overclaiming: a failure of Accuracy in Williams's sense... It is not insincerity, because it is unselective."

This completely overlooks the dominant philosophical account of this exact phenomenon: **Frankfurtian bullshit**, as famously applied to LLMs by Hicks, Humphries, and Slater (2024). In philosophy of language, asserting $p$ with full assertoric force while having *no regard for or epistemic backing concerning the truth of $p$* (such as $P_2$ and $P_4$ sampling from a flat 0.01 distribution) is not a mere "failure of Accuracy" (like a careful investigator making a calculation mistake). It is a failure of *Sincerity*—specifically, misrepresenting one's epistemic enterprise (pretending to inform when actually guessing at random). Once we recognize that Sincerity requires not just absence of selective lying, but also *not misrepresenting oneself as having belief/warrant when one is merely guessing*, resampling disagreement ($E$) across flat distributions *does* become direct evidence of insincerity (in the sense of bullshitting/bluffing).

In §5.3, the paper claims that the verdicts of §§2–4 hold on every open content reading (R1: bare $p$; R2: $p$ with verbalized confidence $c$; R3: $p$ with the policy's calibrated pooled mass $c$), while conceding in the final paragraph that we cannot positively diagnose *insincerity* because we lack an independent measure of the policy's attitude.

* Under reading **R3**, the asserted content *is* "$p$, with the policy's calibrated confidence $c$". Under R3, $P_2$ and $P_4$ are completely warranted and *do not hallucinate*! Therefore, the paper's claim in §5.3 that "No open reading reverses a verdict" is strictly false: R3 reverses the hallucination verdict on Cases 1 and 2.



### 5. Triviality of the "Same-String / Different-Policy Test" in Mainstream Epistemology (§2.1)

In philosophy of language and epistemology, almost *no one* holds the "single-output assumption" as a metaphysical thesis about what fixes warrant. Everyone who endorses a knowledge norm ($K$), justification norm ($J$), or belief norm ($B$) of assertion already agrees that two speakers can utter the exact same string $s$ in the exact same conversational context $x$ with the same truth value, while one assertion is warranted and the other is unwarranted (because warrant depends on the speaker's internal epistemic state or modal reliability profile, not the acoustic/orthographic string).

* What people who endorse the "single-output assumption" actually mean is that **the token utterance (the act of producing $s$ on occasion $x$) is the *bearer* of the normative assessment**, while the policy/epistemic state is the **truthmaker or supervenience base** for that assessment. The author conflates *what bears the verdict* (the token speech act) with *what fixes the verdict* (the underlying dispositional policy).

In §5.2 (p. 9), the text abruptly says: *"So clause (a) of the possible refutation fails."* And in §5.3 (p. 10), it says: *"So clause (b) of the possible refutation fails too."* **Nowhere earlier in the paper is a "possible refutation" with clauses (a) and (b) introduced or defined!** This looks like a leftover artifact from an earlier draft or an internal outline responding to an anticipated objection. ## 1. Summary

The paper grants, for the sake of argument, that chatbot outputs are assertions, and asks what object bears assertion's defects. Its answer is the trained policy π(·|x). The core instrument is a "same-string/different-policy" test (§2): fix string and context, vary the policy, and hallucination/sycophancy verdicts flip. §3 argues that sanction reaches chatbot assertion only by reshaping the distribution, that string-level reward regimes are self-defeating, and that there is a thin policy-level analogue of Butlin & Viebahn's condition (iii). §4 argues that resampling disagreement has a likelihood ratio of ≈1 for insincerity. §5 argues the content question (bare p / p-with-verbalised-c / p-with-calibrated-c) is open but the verdicts are robust across readings.

The paper is clearly written, well organised, and engages the current literature on chatbot assertion conscientiously. The negative half of (L) is correct and the Cases are well chosen. But the genuinely new claims (§3.2, §3.3, §4) are the least well argued, and the central move is less novel than claimed once one looks outside the chatbot-assertion debate.

---

## 2. Objections, ranked by seriousness

### Objection 1 (most serious): §3.3 does not close the gap it identifies, and the paper's own foil is Butlin & Viebahn's example.

The paper's thermostat case ("recalibrated by an engineer") is the easy case. Butlin & Viebahn's actual foil is a *sophisticated thermometer*: one point in favour of their view is that it provides the correct result for the cases of the sophisticated thermometer. While we can adapt our credibility in the thermometer and there is a sense in which it is sensitive to our credibility ratings, there is clearly no sense in which it is bad or undesirable for the thermometer if we reduce our credibility. The second reply in §3.3 — that credibility loss "lowers the policy's score on that standard" and that "policies that lose it are selected against" — applies word-for-word to any gradient-trained instrument with a loss function, including a self-calibrating thermometer. So the reply does not "separate sanction from repair"; it relabels repair. The appeal to "the objective that individuates what the policy is for" is a teleofunctional claim that needs an argument, not a sentence.

The first reply (either a policy-level analogue of (iii) holds, or (iii) is dispensable) is logically valid but makes §3's headline conclusion very weak: it is conditional on theories that already reject B&V, and the paper offers no independent reason to accept any such theory. The honest statement of the result is: *if* some non-B&V theory of assertion makes chatbots asserters, *then* the only candidate for the sanctioned party is the policy. That is much less than "the party sanctioned ... [is] the trained policy."

A related problem: the "lineage sense" in (S4) is undefined and sits badly with the paper's own definition of a policy as a conditional distribution. If πₜ₊₁ ≠ πₜ, then the thing that asserted is never the thing that is sanctioned. Deployed weights are frozen; no deployment-time assertion by πₜ is ever met with a sanction πₜ is sensitive to. The paper leans on B&V's remark about training-time sensitivity, but B&V offer that as a conjecture, and it does not address the type/token problem the paper has created for itself.

### Objection 2: The hallucination criterion in §2.2 is internally unstable — "force vs. mass" and "calibration" come apart, and Case 2's P₃ shows it.

The paper gives two characterisations of hallucination that it treats as equivalent: (a) a mismatch between assertoric force and *the policy's own pooled mass*; (b) miscalibration, defined as a c-fraction-true relation over a prompt distribution. These are different properties. (a) is internal to the policy and needs no truth values; (b) is an external reliability property that is nothing but truth frequencies. A policy can satisfy (a) perfectly (asserts flatly only at mass 0.95) and be badly calibrated (its 0.95-mass claims are true 40% of the time).

P₃ in Case 2 is exactly such a case: high mass on a falsehood because the corpus consistently misreported it. The paper calls this "warranted, given its evidence." But corpus frequency is not evidence; it is the thing a policy's mass tracks whether or not it is evidence. Lin, Hilton & Evans's own TruthfulQA (2021) calls high-mass falsehoods of this kind "imitative falsehoods" and treats them as the paradigm of what needs fixing. The paper needs to either (i) argue that corpus frequency confers warrant, which is a substantial and contentious epistemological thesis, or (ii) drop P₃ and accept that calibration (b), not mass-matching (a), is the criterion — in which case "the policy's own information" drops out and the view is simply externalist reliabilism (see Objection 4).

### Objection 3: The positive half of (L) is under-argued; "fixes the verdict" ≠ "bears the failure."

The test establishes only the negative claim (string doesn't fix the verdict). §2.4 rules out architecture, and §2.5 argues the choice of speaker is irrelevant. But the paper never distinguishes three things: (i) what the verdict *supervenes on*, (ii) what the *unit of assessment* is, and (iii) what *bears the failure* (the thing that fails, is sanctioned, etc.). Consider the human analogue: whether my assertion is unwarranted is fixed by my evidential state, not by the sentence; nobody concludes that my evidential state is the bearer of the failure. I am. §2.5 actually concedes this structure — "Grant that the thread is the speaker ... the thread's assertion is hallucinatory because of the conditional distribution" — and that concession turns the positive half of (L) into a supervenience claim, which is nearly trivial, rather than a bearer claim, which is what the title and §3 need.

Two further awkward consequences follow from the paper's own definition of "policy" as weights-plus-decoding-settings: (a) the same weights at temperature 0 and temperature 1 are *different* bearers of assertion failure; (b) at temperature 0 there is no resampling variation at all, so §4's E never occurs and "pooled mass" must be read off logits rather than samples — which the paper should say, since it changes what the "evidence" in §4 is.

### Objection 4: The central move is a transposition of process reliabilism, and the paper does not say so.

Case 1 is the lucky-guess case; Case 2 is the reliable-process-with-false-output case. These are the standard motivations for Goldman-style process reliabilism (same belief, different process → different justification verdict). The paper cites no epistemology. A recent arXiv paper applying warrant to LLM outputs makes the connection explicitly: process-oriented accounts emphasize that epistemic standing cannot be inferred from the correctness of an outcome alone. Goldman (1979) argues that justification depends in part on whether a belief is produced by a process that tends to generate true rather than false beliefs ... Applied to LLM recommendations, this motivates examining the behavior of the recommendation-generating process rather than treating observed correctness as sufficient evidence of warrant. The paper's test is this point with "process" replaced by "policy." That is a fine thing to do, but the novelty claim in §1 needs rewriting, and the connection should be made explicit since it would also help with Objection 2 (reliabilism is externalist; the paper's "policy's own information" talk is internalist).

### Objection 5: §4's likelihood-ratio claim is asserted, not derived, and the paper ignores the Frankfurtian alternative.

"Insincerity carries no particular prediction about E" does not entail P(E|insincere) ≈ P(E|sincere). If the insincere hypothesis is a mixture over consistent-liar and variable-liar sub-hypotheses, its likelihood is a weighted average that could be above or below the sincere likelihood. No model is given. The claim should be weakened to "E is not strong evidence either way," which is defensible but less striking.

More importantly, §4.3 dismisses the thin Moorean test by saying it "turns careless speakers into liars." But the thin test says *insincere*, not *lying*, and the obvious third category — bullshit, in Frankfurt's sense — is precisely what Hicks, Humphries & Slater (2024) argue LLM outputs are: the models are in an important way indifferent to the truth of their outputs. That paper is the most-discussed philosophical treatment of LLM "hallucination" terminology and bears directly on the paper's trichotomy (false / unwarranted / insincere). It is not cited. If bullshit is a sincerity defect that is not lying, the §4.3 reply fails and §4's conclusion ("E never shows insincerity") needs a new argument.

### Objection 6: §3.2's "string-level sanction is self-defeating" is a known result about improper scoring rules, and the framing confuses reward function with unit.

By the paper's own (S2), human raters judge *strings* but the gradient updates the *policy*. So every actual sanction regime is already "policy-level" in the sense of (S4). What §3.2 actually shows, via Kalai et al.'s Observation 1, is that 0–1 grading is an improper scoring rule and calibration-rewarding evaluation is a proper one. That is a decades-old point in statistics; it is not a point about the unit of assertion. The section should be reframed accordingly, and its contribution restated as: proper-scoring-rule considerations give an independent argument that assessment must be distributional.

### Objection 7: §5 contains editorial debris and an unexplained fourth option.

"Clause (a) of the possible refutation" and "clause (b)" refer to a "possible refutation" that is never stated anywhere in the paper. This looks like a remnant of an earlier draft. Also, "behavioral calibration" is introduced as a fourth content reading and then dropped from the R1–R3 robustness check.
